While Apple has long made privacy a selling point for its hardware and services, I am genuinely curious whether it now regrets introducing one privacy measure: App Tracking Transparency (ATT).

For a feature with a fairly limited scope, it sometimes feels like there's a new antitrust lawsuit or regulatory challenge almost every month and it never stops. The UK is brewing its third ATT lawsuit — and this time there's something new.

This article has been updated to include Apple's response at the end……

Personalised Advertising Controversy

Personalised advertising has been a hotly debated topic in tech for years. Instead of seeing random ads we may or may not be interested in, we now see ads selected based on our interests — interests collected from the apps we use and the websites we browse.

In theory, this is good for everyone. Consumers see ads they might actually be interested in; advertisers get better returns on their ad spend because the ads are more targeted; and meanwhile, ad-funded free apps and websites earn more revenue for the same reason.

Although the data used to deliver personalised ads is collected anonymously, the practice is widely perceived as a privacy invasion. Even though Apple specifically developed technology to ensure this data remains anonymous, many consumers remain sceptical.

App Tracking Transparency

Apple's App Tracking Transparency (ATT) was intended to address this issue by giving consumers a choice over whether their data could be used to serve personalised ads. Developers wishing to collect this data must first obtain the consumer's consent.

Unfortunately for the iPhone maker, this measure has triggered a string of lawsuits and antitrust investigations, mainly because Apple's own apps do not need to seek such consent. Apple has repeatedly stressed that its rules are actually consistent: its own apps don't show the ATT prompt because they don't collect the data ATT covers. Third-party apps that don't collect the relevant data are similarly exempt and don't need to show the prompt either.

The Latest UK Lawsuit

So far, Apple has faced three complaints before the UK's relevant antitrust regulator — the Competition Appeal Tribunal. It lost the first one — though the case is currently under appeal — and the second is still ongoing.

Reuters reported on the third, which was filed today.

What's New

The latest lawsuit has an interesting twist: the plaintiff is Ann Pope, a former senior official at the regulator behind the case.

Ann Pope, a former senior official at the UK's Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), is leading the lawsuit. She says Apple's policy "has caused very significant harm to businesses that rely on Apple as a gatekeeper." Pope said in a statement: "This action is vital to protect the rights of UK businesses that depend on Apple, to ensure the rules Apple applies are fair, and to compensate UK companies for the losses they have suffered."

Earlier, after an investigation by Germany's antitrust regulator, Apple agreed to make eight changes to its ATT rules across the EU. Regarding the current lawsuit, the company responded to us as follows:

Over the years, many privacy advocates have publicly voiced their support for ATT.
